title: A pricing page for a consumer brand
metaTitle: A pricing page shoppers can judge
excerpt: Show the price, the unit, what is included, and what is not, next to a way to see the product. Shoppers judge fit from that shape, and they will ask if you hide it.
alt: Curved library shelves packed with books, seen from a balcony. A catalog you can scan, which is the job of a clear price.
caption: Curved library shelves packed with books, seen from a balcony. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What is the shape of a product price?
faqs.answer: The shape is the number, the unit, what arrives with it, and what does not, including shipping, duties, or a refill if those change the decision. Put make time next to the price when the object is made to order. A shopper is buying the wait as well as the thing.

faqs.question: Should a set make the shopper do the arithmetic?
faqs.answer: Count the pieces on the page and show whether buying them separately costs more. Do that sum once. A shopper who has to open three products to understand a bundle is doing work the brand already did.

faqs.question: Where should the price live so it stays true?
faqs.answer: In one system that every page reads. A banner with a hard-coded discount will drift from the product page. If you discount, do it where the price lives, with an end, and show a comparison only when the original price was real.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?
Influencing Title Links in Google Search

markdown:
A consumer brand pricing page is how a shopper who does not know you judges fit. Show what the price includes, what it leaves out, and a way to see the product. Put the shape of the price on the page. People will ask, and a missing number feels like a game.

Fit here is simple. Can I afford this object, do I understand what arrives, and can I look at the thing itself before I commit. The page should finish those questions. It should not turn them into correspondence.

## The shape of the price, in one glance

Lead with the object name, the price, and the unit. A mug at a single price. A jacket in a small size run, with the price stable across sizes if that is true, or with the difference shown if it is not. A refill sold separately from the bottle. The unit matters as much as the currency. "From" is acceptable only when the range is printed beside it, and the cheapest item is something you are proud to sell.

Say the tax posture in the same glance if your shoppers are split across regions. Tax included, or tax added at checkout, stated in a line under the number. A price that jumps at the last step feels like a different brand from the careful one you showed on the homepage. The homepage promised an object. The price should feel like part of that object.

Nielsen Norman Group notes that people often leave a page within 10 to 20 seconds unless the value is obvious in about 10, in its article on [how long users stay](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/). On a pricing page the value is the number and the unit. A paragraph about craft above a hidden price spends the 10 seconds on the maker. Show the number. Let the craft sit underneath, where the convinced shopper will still read a fraction of it. The same research says they read about a quarter of the text anyway.

If you have a small set, a simple table can carry the line: product, what it is, price, what is included. If you have a large catalog, the pricing "page" may be the price component on every product page, held to one pattern. The pattern is the point. A shopper who learns your prices in one place should recognize them in the next.

## What the price includes

Write the included list in physical terms. The object. The pouch. A spare filter. Gift wrap on request. Shipping above a threshold, if that is the rule, with the threshold printed. Engraving, if engraving is actually available and the characters are limited. A note on the material that justifies care, such as "unglazed foot, so use a coaster," belongs near the price because it changes use, and use changes whether the price feels fair.

Sets need the contents counted. A three-piece set should say three, and should say whether buying the pieces separately costs more. Do the arithmetic once on the page. A shopper who has to open three products to learn the bundle is doing work the brand already did in a spreadsheet.

Subscriptions and refills need the cadence. Every eight weeks. Cancel before the next renewal. The price of the refill against the price of the starter. A starter price that only makes sense with a subscription should say that in the same size as the number. Quiet hope that they will not notice is a weak commercial strategy, and it is a fast way to lose the second order.

Pre-order and made-to-order change what "buy" means. State the make time next to the price. "Ships in four weeks" is part of the price shape, because the shopper is buying a wait as well as an object. A surprise wait after payment is a support ticket you wrote yourself.

## What the price does not include

Exclusions make the included list believable. Shipping under the threshold, with the typical cost or a link to the exact table. Duties for international orders, if the shopper pays them on arrival. A battery, a bulb, a frame, a second colorway that is a different product. Personalization that looks included in the photograph and is actually extra.

Returns belong in a sentence beside the price. Thirty days, unworn, at your cost or theirs. A shopper who cannot find the return rule will either leave or assume the worst. Assuming the worst is a tax on a brand that was trying to seem careful. One accurate sentence beats a policy novel linked from the footer only.

If a product is final sale, say final sale next to the price, not in a tooltip. Final sale is a boundary. Hiding it until confirmation is how trust breaks. The same goes for items cut to order. People accept a firm rule. They resent a soft page that becomes firm at the end.

Samples, if you offer them, are a pricing product too. A paid swatch credited against the order. A free swatch with a posted limit. Say which. An unlabeled "request a sample" button with no cost and no timing is an unfinished price.

## See the product from the price

Every price should be attached to a way to see the product. A photograph at a useful scale, a link to more views, the sizes or volumes in plain text. The pricing page fails if it becomes a spreadsheet divorced from the object. The shopper is judging fit, which includes "is this the thing I saw on the homepage."

Use the same name in both places. If the homepage said Coast mug, the price line says Coast mug. Synonyms feel like a catalog error. They are a small crack in a brand that otherwise asks to be trusted with materials and money.

Variants sit under the price, not in a separate philosophy. Color, size, and scent as choices with their own pictures when the picture would change. If a variant is out of stock, show it as unavailable and keep the price visible, so the shopper learns the shape even when they cannot buy today. A vanished variant looks like the brand is hiding the cost of the desirable version.

Down the Cove, a public Hanabi project, is an ecommerce restructure, migration, and redesign. The pricing lesson from that kind of shop work is continuity. People should still recognize the goods and the price logic after a redesign. A new skin that obscures the number is a step backward, however calm the type is.

## Keep one source of the number

The price lives in one system, and every page reads it. A campaign banner that hard-codes a discount will drift from the product page by Friday. If you discount, do it in the same place the price lives, with an end, and show the original only if the original was real and recent. A fictional comparison price is a costume. Serious shops get caught.

Regional prices, if you use them, should be deliberate. A shopper who travels between two of your sites and sees unexplained gaps will assume the higher one is a trick. If the gap is shipping or tax, say so. If the gap is a different wholesale reality, you still owe a sentence a human can read.

Editors need to change a number without a developer when the cost of goods changes. Build the price as content. On a custom shop, that is a reasonable requirement of the build. Hanabi's ecommerce work treats the catalog as something the team can keep true after launch. The number is the most sensitive true thing you have.

Gift cards and wholesale rates can have their own lines. They should not take over the page a retail shopper came to read. Link wholesale to its own path if the terms are different enough to confuse a person buying one mug. Two audiences on one price table produce a table neither will finish.

## A title that says this is the price

Name the page, or the block, as the price. "Coast mug" as the heading and the price directly under it. Google's guidance on [title links](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/title-link) favors descriptive titles and warns against boilerplate that makes every page sound the same. "Shop – Brand Name" on every product throws away the chance to say which object and, where it helps, that the page holds the price. A specific title also helps the shopper who has twelve tabs open.

The visible heading and the title should match. If the heading is poetic and the price is the only concrete fact, adjust the heading until the object and the price are what the page claims to be. Poetry can be the second line.

When the price changes, change the page the same day. A screenshot will outlive your intention. If a waitlist or a pre-order window closes, close it visibly. Leaving a buy button active for a product you cannot make is a pricing error, because the price included an implied delivery.

## From the number to the offer it belongs to

A price makes sense when the shopper knows which offer they are in. The object, the set, the refill, the made-to-order piece. If those offers are still a grid of vague names, the next page to fix is the one that lists them in the shopper's language, each with an outcome, a boundary, and a way to see the product. That is [the services page a consumer brand actually needs](/blog/the-services-page-a-consumer-brand-actually-needs).

For help putting the price and the product on speaking terms, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). Bring the real price list, including the exclusions you usually explain in email.
